title: Tackling Low Participation Tasks
author: Peter Foster
summary: Peter Foster argues that two activities teachers assume are cognitively engaging, note-taking and reading, are often much less so, and offers concrete redesigns for each. On note-taking, he observes that 'put this in your own words' almost always produces disguised copying, since students report finding copying relaxing precisely because it doesn't require thought; his fix is to design tasks that require comparison, ranking, or interaction with content rather than transcription, and to trust a spoken explanation rather than relying on dense, text-heavy slides students split attention across. He specifically flags copying definitions as a false economy, since copying a definition doesn't teach what a word means the way using it in constructed sentences does. On reading, he distinguishes reading from teaching, arguing there's no guarantee students are attending to what's read without deliberate pauses, and recommends chunking reading around key moments (new terms, callbacks to prior content, ambiguous language) using check-for-comprehension questions or brief turn-and-talks, while warning against turn-and-talks that run too long or lack a specific prompt. He closes by reframing high participation as something to pursue continuously throughout a lesson rather than something achieved only during designated 'high participation' activities.
points: Foster's core claim is that 'put this into your own words' almost always produces disguised copying, since students themselves report finding copying easier and more relaxing precisely because it requires no thought.
He specifically singles out copying definitions as a false economy, arguing that copying a definition doesn't teach word meaning the way constructing and using sentences with the word does.

His reading fix chunks text around specific trigger moments, new terms, callbacks, ambiguous language, rather than either reading straight through or stopping arbitrarily to ask generic comprehension questions.

He sets hard constraints on turn-and-talk (thirty seconds maximum, a specific prompt rather than 'have a chat'), naming vagueness and excessive length as the two most common ways it fails to produce real participation.
quotes: Almost every time a teacher says ‘Put this into your own words’ or ‘Make some notes’, the students copy whatever they’re given.
Students aren’t thinking when they’re copying as much as we’d like to believe they are. And, in getting them to copy, we’re outsourcing (or maybe abdicating) our responsibility to teach them.
Copying a definition is not the same as teaching students what a word means.
Reading is an undeniable good and, of course, often absolutely essential. But reading, like note-taking, is not the same as teaching.
The biggest mistakes with turn and talk are: Making it too long. It should be thirty seconds at the maximum.
Ultimately, it’s worth trying to move past seeing high participation as tied to certain types of task; instead, we aim to eke out as much participation from every part of the lesson as possible.
